facts.summary: Georgia has no state overtime statute; the federal FLSA governs, requiring 1.5x pay after 40 hours in a workweek with no daily overtime and no higher state salary floor.
facts.citation: O.C.G.A. Title 34 (no state overtime provision); 29 U.S.C. 207
facts.notes: Georgia enacts no state overtime law; the DOL page directs to the FLSA (29 U.S.C.) for wage-and-hour coverage. Verify no new state overtime rule each year.

facts.summary: Georgia's statutory minimum wage is $5.15/hour, but with limited exceptions the higher federal minimum wage of $7.25/hour applies to most covered employees.
facts.notes: State figure of $5.15 is below federal; employees covered by the FLSA must receive $7.25. State rate unchanged for years; confirm current-year figure.

facts.summary: Under Georgia's Fair Employment Practices Act the state (via GCEO) prohibits discrimination on race, color, religion, national origin, sex including sexual orientation, age, and disability.
facts.notes: GCEO lists sex 'including sexual orientation' consistent with Bostock. Classes largely mirror the federal set; the notable state feature is the narrow employer coverage (see discrimination.coverage), not additional classes.

facts.summary: Georgia's Fair Employment Practices Act reaches only State of Georgia government agencies; it does not cover private employers, counties, or municipalities, so private-sector discrimination claims proceed under federal law (EEOC).
facts.citation: O.C.G.A. § 45-19-20 et seq. (Fair Employment Practices Act)
facts.notes: GCEO's Equal Employment Division enforces FEPA only for those seeking or holding employment within Georgia state government. FEPA statutorily applies to state agencies with 15 or more employees; GCEO pages do not restate the size threshold, so verify the 15-employee figure against O.C.G.A. § 45-19-22 before relying on it.

facts.summary: A discrimination complaint under Georgia's Fair Employment Practices Act must be filed in writing (sworn) with the GCEO within 180 calendar days of the alleged unlawful employment practice.
facts.citation: O.C.G.A. § 45-19-20 et seq. (Fair Employment Practices Act)
facts.notes: 180-day deadline confirmed on GCEO filing pages. Applies to state-government employment claims only; private-sector claimants use the EEOC's 180/300-day federal deadlines.

facts.summary: Georgia's Whistleblower Act bars public employers from retaliating against public employees who disclose or refuse to participate in violations of law, rule, or regulation.
facts.sourceAgency: Georgia Office of the Inspector General
facts.notes: Protects public (government) employees only; no equivalent general private-sector state whistleblower statute. Statute provides a civil action in superior court (reported as within 1 year of discovering the retaliation, or 3 years of the retaliation, whichever is earlier) - verify the exact limitation period in O.C.G.A. § 45-1-4(e) as the source PDF could not be machine-read.

facts.value: no dedicated overtime/wage-claim limitations period under state law; a separate 3-year civil action exists only for underpayment below Georgia's own (lower) statutory minimum wage
facts.summary: Georgia has no general state wage-and-hour statute or limitations period; unpaid-wage and overtime claims in Georgia are almost always brought under the federal FLSA. A narrow state action for paying an employee less than Georgia's own statutory minimum wage must be brought within 3 years.
facts.citation: O.C.G.A. § 34-4-6 (state minimum-wage shortfall action only); 29 U.S.C. § 255 (FLSA, generally applicable in Georgia)
facts.notes: Georgia has no state overtime law and no dedicated wage-claim statute of limitations; most wage/overtime disputes are litigated under the federal FLSA (2 years, 3 if willful - see the federal deadlines.wageClaim fact). O.C.G.A. § 34-4-6 separately allows a 3-year civil action to recover the shortfall when an employer pays less than Georgia's own (lower, $5.15) statutory minimum wage, but the Department of Labor's page does not display the statute text itself; the 3-year figure could not be confirmed on a directly linkable official government page and should be verified against the Official Code of Georgia before relying on it.
